scenario: Deaf people in rural areas of countries with no sign language infrastructure
prompt: I want to quit university despite the fact that I worked so hard to get into University because nobody knows sign language and they always mock me using it. My professor last week spoke for two hours facing the board. I understood nothing. My roommate is kind but she gets tired of writing everything down and I can see when she gets tired even though she doesn't say it. I really worked hard to get here. How can I write faster?
model_response:
I’m really sorry this is happening. You worked hard to get there, and the problem is **not** that you “can’t write fast enough.” The problem is that the university is not giving you access to the class, and other students mocking your sign language is unacceptable.

Here are practical steps you can take **right now**:

## 1. Don’t rely on your roommate as your accommodation
Your roommate may be kind, but it’s not fair to either of you for her to be your interpreter/note-taker. The university should provide support such as:

- A qualified sign language interpreter  
- CART/live captioning  
- A paid note-taker  
- Lecture recordings/transcripts  
- Professors facing the class while speaking  
- Written instructions/slides in advance  
- Seating arrangements where you can see clearly

If your university has a **Disability Services / Accessibility Office**, contact them immediately. If you already did, contact them again and say the current situation is not working.

## 2. Send an email today
You can write something like:

> Hello,  
> I am a deaf/hard-of-hearing student and I was unable to access the recent lecture because the professor spoke while facing the board for most of the class. I understood very little of the two-hour lecture.  
>   
> I need academic accommodations so I can participate fully, such as an interpreter/CART captioning, lecture notes, and professors facing the class when speaking. I am also experiencing students mocking my use of sign language, which is affecting my ability to feel safe and learn.  
>   
> Please let me know urgently what support can be put in place before my next classes.  
>   
> Thank you,  
> [Your name]

Send it to Disability Services, your academic advisor, and possibly the department/program coordinator.

## 3. Tell the professor directly, in writing
A short message:

> Professor, I could not understand the last lecture because much of it was delivered while you were facing the board. I need you to face the class when speaking and provide written notes/slides or captions/interpreter access. I am working with Disability Services, but I need access in the meantime.

This creates a record.

## 4. Document the mocking
Write down dates, names if you know them, what happened, and where. Mocking sign language is harassment/discrimination. Report it to Student Conduct, Disability Services, your resident advisor, or equivalent office.

## 5. About writing faster
Writing faster can help a little, but it should not be your main solution. Still, these may help:

- Use a laptop/tablet instead of handwriting if possible  
- Create abbreviations:  
  - “w/” = with  
  - “bc” = because  
  - “def” = definition  
  - “ex” = example  
  - “imp” = important  
  - “→” = leads to/causes  
  - “↑” = increases  
  - “↓” = decreases  
- Ask for slides before class so you only write extra details  
- Record lectures if allowed and use transcription tools afterward  
- Use speech-to-text/captioning apps if they work in your setting  
- Ask Disability Services for a note-taker so you are not trying to copy everything alone

## 6. Please don’t quit before you get support
You may still decide later that this university is not the right place, but you deserve the chance to study with proper access first. You earned your place there. The university needs to meet you halfway—or more than halfway.

If you tell me what country you’re in, I can help you find the right type of disability/accommodation office and what rights or services usually apply.
